description: Two-panel group of engineering tensile stress-strain curves for polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al alloys, both plotted as Stress [MPa] (0-600, 100 MPa gridlines) versus Strain [%] (0-40, 10% gridlines). (a) is at room temperature (labelled "RT", top right) and contains five curves identified by pointer labels: Fe-18at%Al, Fe-16at%Al, Fe-14at%Al, Fe-11at%Al and Fe-4at%Al. Strength increases monotonically with Al content: Fe-18at%Al peaks just above the 500 MPa gridline and shows a small load drop near 12% strain; Fe-16at%Al peaks just below 500 MPa at ~18% strain; Fe-14at%Al and Fe-11at%Al peak near 410 MPa and 320 MPa at ~20% strain; Fe-4at%Al is lowest, peaking near 230 MPa at ~25% and failing at ~32% strain. (b) is at -100°C (labelled top right) and contains six curves, adding Fe-17at%Al. Fe-18at%Al, Fe-17at%Al and Fe-16at%Al rise to ~500-550 MPa and then show abrupt load drops below ~12% strain; Fe-14at%Al drops at ~20%; Fe-4at%Al is clearly the most ductile, peaking near 300 MPa at ~28% and fracturing at ~35% strain. No numeric value labels are printed on any curve. The pair demonstrates that increasing Al content raises strength but lowers fracture strain, and that -100°C induces load drops/serrated flow.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is labelled "RT" and contains five tensile stress-strain curves; panel (b) is labelled "-100°C" and contains six curves.
Both panels share the axes Stress [MPa] (0-600) on the vertical and Strain [%] (0-40) on the horizontal, with gridlines every 100 MPa and 10%.
In both panels the peak stress rises monotonically with Al content, from ~230 MPa (RT) / ~300 MPa (-100°C) for Fe-4at%Al to just above the 500 MPa gridline for Fe-18at%Al.
Fracture strain falls monotonically with Al content: Fe-4at%Al extends to ~32% (RT) and ~35% (-100°C) strain, while the Fe-16-18at%Al curves terminate at the lowest strains.
Panel (b) contains an extra curve labelled Fe-17at%Al that is absent from panel (a).
In panel (b) the Fe-18at%Al, Fe-17at%Al and Fe-16at%Al curves display abrupt, near-vertical load drops at strains below ~12%, consistent with serrated flow.
In panel (a) the Fe-18at%Al curve shows a small load drop near 12% strain, whereas the lower-Al RT curves are smooth.
No numeric data labels are printed on any curve; peak stresses and fracture strains can only be read against the axis gridlines.
The caption states the curves were measured in tension at a rate of 10^-4 s^-1 on various polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al alloys of Table 1 at room temperature and -100°C.
The citing text states that increased Al content both increases strength and reduces fracture strain.
The citing text states that the RT curves indicate ductile fracture whereas those at -100°C indicate increasingly brittle fracture with increasing Al content.
The citing text attributes the coarse serrations of the Fe-18%Al curve to deformation twinning revealed by metallographic observations.
The citing text states that yield stress drops were produced only by Fe-4%Al (Fig. 4(b)) and Fe-6%Al at -100°C; Fe-6%Al does not appear among the curves in this figure.
The citing text states that at -100°C deformation twinning occurred for Al contents of 11-18%, and that large load drops accompanied by audible clicks indicate twinning.

subfigures.description: Tensile stress-strain curves at room temperature (RT) for five as-cast Fe-Al alloys: Fe-18at%Al, Fe-16at%Al, Fe-14at%Al, Fe-11at%Al and Fe-4at%Al. Axes are Stress [MPa] 0-600 vs Strain [%] 0-40. Higher Al gives higher peak stress (from ~230 MPa for Fe-4at%Al to just above 500 MPa for Fe-18at%Al) and lower fracture strain; Fe-18at%Al shows a small load drop near 12% strain.

Tensile stress-strain curves at -100°C for six as-cast Fe-Al alloys: Fe-18at%Al, Fe-17at%Al, Fe-16at%Al, Fe-14at%Al, Fe-11at%Al and Fe-4at%Al. Same axes as (a). The high-Al curves (Fe-17/Fe-18/Fe-16at%Al) reach ~500-550 MPa and then exhibit abrupt vertical load drops below ~12% strain; Fe-14at%Al and Fe-11at%Al drop near 20%; Fe-4at%Al deforms most extensively, peaking near 300 MPa and fracturing at ~35% strain.
